Weapons-usable material is the rare exception: 13 confirmed high-enriched-uranium cases and 3 plutonium cases across 32 years, and the last seizure of kilogram quantities of weapons-usable nuclear material was in 1994.
published.name: Nuclear and Radiological Material Out of Regulatory Control

assessment.summary: Thousands of warheads remain in military stockpiles — thousands deployed, and roughly two thousand on high alert — making nuclear war a persistent, low-probability, civilization-scale risk, now with no bilateral treaty capping the two largest arsenals since New START lapsed in February 2026.
assessment.timeframe: No reliable forecast; risk tracks geopolitical crises, arsenal modernization, and the erosion or renewal of arms-control agreements — the last US-Russia strategic treaty lapsed in February 2026.

claims.text: SIPRI estimates a total global inventory of 12,187 nuclear warheads in January 2026, of which about 9,745 were in military stockpiles for potential use.

An estimated 4,012 warheads were deployed with missiles and aircraft in January 2026, and between 2,100 and 2,200 of the deployed warheads were kept in a state of high operational alert on ballistic missiles.
Nine states possess nuclear weapons: the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, China, India, Pakistan, North Korea and Israel.
Russia and the USA together possess around 83 per cent of all stockpiled nuclear warheads.

With the expiry of the bilateral 2010 Treaty on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms (New START) in February 2026, uncertainty is increasing about the future direction of US and Russian strategic nuclear force levels (SIPRI Yearbook 2026).

published.description: A deliberate or inadvertent nuclear exchange between states. Global arsenals remain in the thousands of warheads — about 9,745 of an estimated 12,187 held in military stockpiles for potential use in January 2026, some 4,012 of them deployed and between 2,100 and 2,200 kept on high operational alert. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their forces, and Russia and the United States alone hold roughly 83 percent of stockpiled warheads. New START, the last bilateral treaty capping their strategic forces, expired in February 2026 with no replacement, leaving the future direction of US and Russian strategic force levels newly uncertain.
published.name: Nuclear War

assessment.summary: A measured, ongoing shift in ocean chemistry — surface pH already down about 0.1 unit since pre-industrial times, roughly a 30% rise in acidity — projected to fall a further 0.3–0.4 units by 2100, eroding the calcifying species at the base of marine food webs and the fisheries built on them.
assessment.timeframe: Already underway and directly measured in ocean time series; the projected additional 0.3–0.4 pH decline runs to 2100, and surface-ocean chemistry takes thousands of years to recover once emissions stop.

claims.text: NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory states that the ocean's pH at the sea surface once measured at 8.2 before the 1700s and today is estimated at 8.1, a 0.1 decrease in ocean pH.

NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory states that since the Industrial Revolution the global average pH of the surface ocean has decreased by 0.11, which corresponds to approximately a 30% increase in hydrogen ion concentration.
The Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO states that every year the ocean absorbs about 25% of human-made carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions.

NOAA Fisheries states that over the past 200 years the world's oceans have absorbed more than 150 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emitted from human activities, and that ocean carbon dioxide concentrations are now higher than at any time during the past 800,000 years.
NOAA states that by 2100 the average pH of the ocean's surface waters could decrease by 0.3 to 0.4, a 100% to 150% increase in acidification over the next 75 years.

NOAA states that the predicted pH decrease of approximately 0.3 units during the 21st century would be a greater change than possibly at any time in the last 300 million years, and that when aragonite saturation state falls below 3 calcifying organisms become stressed, while below 1 shells and other aragonite structures begin to dissolve.

NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory reports that oyster seed production in the U.S. Northwest plummeted by as much as 80 percent between 2005 and 2009 as acidified water reached hatcheries, in a Washington shellfish industry worth $270 million a year.

published.description: Ocean acidification is the measured fall in seawater pH caused by the ocean absorbing about a quarter of human carbon dioxide emissions. Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, raising the hydrogen-ion concentration and stripping out the carbonate ions that corals, oysters, clams, pteropods and other calcifying organisms need to build shells and skeletons. Surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 before the 1700s to about 8.1 today — roughly a 30% rise in acidity — and NOAA projects a further decline of 0.3–0.4 units by 2100 on current emissions, a shift larger than possibly any in the last 300 million years. This is not a discrete disaster but a slow, near-irreversible change in the chemistry of the entire ocean: it does not threaten human survival directly, and it acts at the base of marine food webs that supply the primary protein of more than a billion people. Only cutting CO2 emissions slows it; surface-ocean chemistry takes millennia to recover on its own.
published.name: Ocean Acidification

assessment.summary: The cryptography is standardised and the deadlines are set; the open question is deployment. A transition that historically takes a decade or two is being attempted in under ten years across an installed base nobody fully inventories, and the long-lived secrets exposed in the meantime cannot be re-protected retroactively. Severity is bounded by the fact that symmetric cryptography and hash functions survive the quantum threat largely intact, so the failure mode is mass compromise of confidentiality and of trust in digital signatures rather than a loss of all computing security.
assessment.timeframe: Already consequential through harvest-now-decrypt-later collection; NIST deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallows it after 2035, while US federal high value assets and high impact systems must migrate key establishment by 31 December 2030 and digital signatures by 31 December 2031.

claims.text: NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (final, October 2026), states: "NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. The 2030-2035 deprecation window accommodates lower-risk systems and applications with legacy constraints while full migration concludes." Its transition tables list ECDSA, EdDSA and RSA signatures, and DH, MQV and RSA key establishment, as deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035.

NIST IR 8547 states that although the transition is starting before a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer has been built, "Encrypted data remains at risk because of the 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat in which adversaries collect encrypted data now with the goal of decrypting it once quantum technology matures," and notes that "Historically, the journey from algorithm standardization to full integration into information systems can take 10 to 20 years."

NIST IR 8547 states that National Security Memorandum 10 "established 2035 as the target for completing the federal migration to post-quantum cryptography" and that under Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15, US federal agencies must transition high value assets and high impact systems on an accelerated schedule: "These systems must adopt post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by December 31, 2030, and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031."

NIST's announcement of the final report, released 27 October 2026, says that today's encrypted data is already at risk from the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat, and describes NIST IR 8547 as the technical document identifying quantum-vulnerable algorithms among NIST's existing cryptographic standards and the replacement post-quantum standards.

NIST's Post-Quantum Cryptography project page states that in August 2024 NIST released its principal post-quantum standards: FIPS 203, the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM); FIPS 204, the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA); and FIPS 205, the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA). The HQC key encapsulation mechanism and the Falcon digital signature algorithm were selected for ongoing standardization.

published.description: A sufficiently capable quantum computer would break the RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography that secures most internet traffic, financial settlement, software updates and government communications. No such machine is known to exist, but the damage does not wait for one: adversaries can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once the capability arrives, so data with a long confidentiality life is already exposed. NIST published its three post-quantum standards in August 2024 and, in the final version of NIST IR 8547 in October 2026, set the schedule for retiring the vulnerable algorithms: quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography is deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards after 2035. US federal policy moves faster still, requiring the most sensitive systems to adopt post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and post-quantum signatures by 31 December 2031. The risk lies in the gap between those deadlines and the 10 to 20 years NIST says previous cryptographic transitions have historically taken, across an installed base of embedded devices, certificates and protocols that no single authority controls.
published.name: Quantum Break of Public-Key Cryptography

assessment.summary: This is the most certain of the climate threats and the slowest to arrive: the measurement record is unambiguous, the physical commitment is locked in for centuries, and the damage lands disproportionately on small island developing States and low-lying deltas that did little to cause it. The near-term range is well constrained; the tail is not, because marine ice-sheet processes in West Antarctica remain the largest source of deep uncertainty in long-horizon projections. Rated continental rather than civilizational because the harm is concentrated on coasts and unfolds slowly enough for adaptation and relocation, at a cost that falls hardest on states least able to pay it.
assessment.timeframe: Already underway and accelerating, with roughly 0.24 m of further global rise projected by 2050 relative to a 2000 baseline and continued rise for centuries thereafter regardless of near-term emissions.

claims.text: NOAA's State of the Climate in 2025 summary reports: "The average global mean sea level for 2025 set a new record, for the 14th year in a row, rising to 111.2 millimeters above the average for 1993, the year when satellite altimetry measurements began, and was 1.0 plus or minus 0.5 millimeters higher compared to 2024."

The same NOAA report states that globally averaged ocean heat content from the surface to 2000-meters depth reached a record high in 2025, surpassing the previous record set in 2024; that the Greenland Ice Sheet "lost an estimated 129 plus or minus 50 Gigatons of ice overall in 2025"; and that land-based glaciers around the world "continued to lose ice for the 38th consecutive year," with about 41% of the ice lost by glaciers since 1976 occurring in just the last decade.

NASA's sea level portal states that global mean sea level "has risen 6 - 8 inches (15 - 20 centimeters) since 1920" and illustrates the acceleration: "It took 90 years (1902 - 1992) for the global sea level to rise around 10 cm," while "In just the last 30 years (1993 - 2023), that same amount of rise, around 10 cm, happened again."

The NOAA-led interagency Sea Level Rise Technical Report states that the observation-based extrapolated value of global mean sea level increase in 2050 relative to a baseline of 2000 is 0.24 m, with a likely (17th-83rd percentile) range between 0.19 m and 0.29 m; an independent extrapolation from satellite altimeter data over 1993-2021 gives 0.23 m of rise from 2000 to 2050, and the equivalent figure for the contiguous US coastline is 0.38 m, with a likely range of 0.32 m to 0.45 m.

At the UN high-level meeting on sea-level rise on 24 September 2026, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said global sea levels rose by almost six millimetres in 2024, the largest annual increase ever recorded; UN News reports that around 770 million people live less than five metres above the high-tide line, and that without drastic emissions cuts seas could rise by a metre by the end of the century.

On 24 September 2026 world leaders approved the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise, which Member States had finalised the previous month. UN News reports that 770 million people live in coastal areas affected by sea level rise and that a half-metre rise could force between 150 million and 300 million people from their homes.

published.description: Global sea level is rising as the ocean warms and land ice melts, pushing coastlines inland and exposing hundreds of millions of people in low-lying areas. NOAA's State of the Climate in 2025 recorded a global mean sea level 111.2 mm above the 1993 satellite-altimetry baseline, a record for the fourteenth consecutive year and 1.0 plus or minus 0.5 mm above 2024. The drivers are both running: ocean heat content from the surface to 2000 m reached a record high in 2025, the Greenland Ice Sheet lost an estimated 129 plus or minus 50 gigatons of ice, and land glaciers lost mass for a thirty-eighth consecutive year. The pace is also changing: NASA notes that the roughly 10 cm of rise that took 90 years from 1902 to 1992 recurred in the 30 years from 1993 to 2023. NOAA's interagency scenarios project a further 0.24 m of global rise by 2050 relative to 2000. Around 770 million people live less than five metres above the high-tide line, and in September 2026 world leaders approved a UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise. Unlike surface temperature, the commitment is effectively irreversible on human timescales: the ocean keeps rising for centuries after emissions stop.
published.name: Sea-Level Rise and Ice-Sheet Loss

assessment.summary: A present, quantified fiscal squeeze — record external debt stock, the largest net outflow from developing countries in half a century, and 3.4 billion people in states paying more in interest than they spend on health or education — that is tightening as borrowing costs climb: Group of Seven ten-year yields are at their highest in nearly two decades and the global primary deficit is widening rather than closing. A synchronised multi-country default wave remains the tail risk.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing and tightening; the World Bank's International Debt Report tracks the position annually, and the IMF's October 2026 Fiscal Monitor expects global public debt to exceed 100 percent of global GDP by 2030, with the effective average interest cost of government financing rising from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent by 2031.

claims.text: Developing countries paid out $741 billion more in principal and interest on their external debt than they received in new financing between 2022 and 2024, and paid a record $415 billion in interest alone in 2024 (International Debt Report 2025, published 3 December 2025).

The combined external debt of low- and middle-income countries hit an all-time high of $8.9 trillion in 2024, including $1.2 trillion owed by the 78 mainly low-income countries eligible to borrow from the World Bank's International Development Association; developing countries restructured $90 billion in external debt in 2024, more than at any time since 2010.

More than 3.4 billion people now live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on health or education — 100 million more than the previous year — and debt service payments by developing countries soared by $74 billion in a single year, from $847 billion to $921 billion (Confronting the Debt Crisis: 11 Actions to Unlock Sustainable Financing, launched 27 June 2025).

Global public debt rose to just under 94 percent of GDP in 2025 and is set to reach 100 percent by 2029, one year earlier than projected in April 2025 (IMF Fiscal Monitor, April 2026: Fiscal Policy under Pressure: High Debt, Rising Risks).

The IMF's October 2026 Fiscal Monitor expects global public debt to exceed 100 percent of global gross domestic product by 2030; the Group of Seven's average 10-year government bond yield increased by over 1 percentage point between February and September 2026, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades; the effective average interest cost of government financing is projected to rise from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent by 2031; and the global primary deficit is about 3.3 percent of GDP in 2026, against the roughly 2.6 percent it would have to be cut to in order to stabilize the global debt-to-GDP ratio this year.

In just three years, interest payments have increased by almost half - from about 2 to nearly 3 percent of GDP - amounting to trillions of dollars globally that cannot go to education, infrastructure, or other priorities, and debt was already on track to reach World War II-era levels by 2028 (IMF Annual Report 2026).

published.description: A growing share of the world's governments owe more in debt service than they can pay without cutting health, education, and climate spending. The combined external debt of low- and middle-income countries hit an all-time high of $8.9 trillion in 2024, and between 2022 and 2024 those countries paid out $741 billion more in principal and interest than they received in new financing — the largest such gap in at least 50 years. More than 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on health or education, and interest has climbed from about 2 to nearly 3 percent of global GDP in three years. The strain is not confined to poorer economies: global public debt reached just under 94 percent of GDP in 2025, the IMF expects it to pass 100 percent by 2030, and Group of Seven ten-year yields rose more than a percentage point between February and September 2026 to their highest level in nearly two decades. The escalation pathway runs from isolated sovereign defaults to a synchronised wave of restructurings, capital flight, and a lost decade of development spending across dozens of countries at once.
published.name: Sovereign Debt Distress

assessment.summary: A steadily growing, already-tracked debris population in Earth orbit carries a real and rising risk of a self-sustaining collision cascade severe enough to disable critical satellite infrastructure.
assessment.timeframe: Debris accumulation is continuous and tracked in real time; a runaway cascade has no predicted date but becomes more likely as orbital object density rises.

claims.text: NASA's Orbital Debris Program Office states more than 25,000 tracked objects larger than 10 cm orbit Earth, with an estimated 500,000 objects between 1 and 10 cm, and more than 100 million objects larger than 1 mm; as of January 2022 the total mass of orbiting material exceeded 9,000 metric tons.
NASA states the International Space Station maneuvers to avoid a tracked object when the estimated collision probability exceeds 1 in 10,000, which occurs about once a year on average.

NASA describes the Kessler syndrome as a domino effect that can result when objects in intersecting orbits collide at thousands of miles per hour, generating debris that raises the odds of further collisions.

The Satellite Box Score in NASA's Orbital Debris Quarterly News (Volume 30, Issue 1 & 2, July 2026) lists 33,098 objects in Earth orbit cataloged by the U.S. Space Surveillance Network as of 4 May 2026 — 18,189 spacecraft, active and defunct, and 14,909 spent rocket bodies and other cataloged debris.

NASA's Orbital Debris Program Office states that because the orbital debris population follows a power-law size distribution, there is far more millimeter-sized debris (on the order of 100 million) than large, trackable objects (approximately 50,000), so the likelihood of non-catastrophic but mission-ending damage from millimeter-sized debris is orders of magnitude greater than that of an accidental collision with a large, trackable object.

published.description: Decades of launches, spent rocket stages, defunct satellites, and past collisions have left a large and growing population of debris in Earth orbit. As the density of objects in low Earth orbit rises, so does the risk of a cascading chain reaction of collisions — the 'Kessler syndrome' — that could render whole orbital bands too hazardous for satellites and crewed spacecraft for generations, threatening the GPS, communications, weather, and scientific infrastructure the world now depends on. The US Space Surveillance Network now catalogs more than 33,000 objects in orbit, over half of them spacecraft, and NASA estimates on the order of 100 million fragments larger than a millimetre that are too small to track yet still capable of ending a mission. Spacecraft including the International Space Station maneuver away from tracked objects when the collision probability exceeds 1 in 10,000.
published.name: Space Debris and Kessler Syndrome

assessment.summary: The failure rate is not the problem; the concentration and the repair queue are. Several hundred faults a year are absorbed invisibly where a country has many cables and a repair ship nearby, and become a national outage where it has neither. That asymmetry is what the ITU's advisory body was convened to address, and its findings point the wrong way: response times doubling over a decade, a repair fleet of 20-25 genuinely available vessels, and route concentration in chokepoints that no single operator can engineer around. Severity is rated continental rather than civilizational because the physical infrastructure is repairable and redundancy exists in the richest markets; the damage falls on small island developing states, least developed countries and single-cable markets, where the loss of banking, government and health services can last weeks. Deliberate multi-cable sabotage in a chokepoint is the tail risk, and it needs no new capability — a ship and an anchor already account for a quarter of all faults.
assessment.timeframe: Already recurrent — faults occur somewhere in the world every few days and repair response times are lengthening — with the governance response still voluntary after the ITU-ICPC advisory body concluded its work in July 2026.

claims.text: The final report of the ITU-ICPC International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience (Working Group 2, July 2026) states: "Submarine telecommunications cables form the critical backbone of the global digital economy, carrying over 99 per cent of intercontinental data traffic. Despite their strategic importance, however, these networks remain vulnerable to a range of mainly physical risks, experiencing approximately 150-200 faults annually. Over 80 per cent of those incidents are attributable to human maritime activities - primarily commercial fishing and dragged ship anchors."

The same report finds the global repair fleet inadequate: "Given current demand, the global submarine cable repair fleet is insufficient. As of 2025, approximately 70 vessels worldwide possessed the technical capability to perform cable repairs. However, many of these vessels were either primarily for cable-laying and engaged in commercial installation projects, or older units no longer maintained for active service. Only around 20-25 vessels were either formally dedicated to repair operations under active maintenance agreements, or long-term chartered for these."

On repair timelines the report states: "In recent years, the number of repairs per year and the number of repair vessels available have both remained stable, according to the ICPC. However, between 2012 and 2024, the average repair response time more than doubled, from less than 20 days to more than 50 days." It illustrates the geographic gap: "Due to limited resources, there is only one permanent and wholly dedicated cable repair vessel in the whole of Africa. As this is positioned at Cape Town, if a cable fault occurs in the northern part of the continent, the transit will take more than 10 days, regardless of whether the fault is on the east or west coast."

On route concentration the report names chokepoints: "The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern gateway to the Red Sea: This is the most concentrated area in the world, with at least 17 cables - carrying an estimated 17-20 per cent of global Internet traffic - passing through waters less than 14 miles wide" and "The Suez Canal corridor: This funnels an estimated 90 per cent of Europe-Asia communications through waters where cables must traverse shallow depths for over 100 miles before entering the Mediterranean Sea." It attributes 40 per cent of global faults to fishing activity and 25 per cent to anchoring.

ITU announced on 10 July 2026 (Geneva) that the International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience, established in 2024 by ITU and the International Cable Protection Committee, approved its final report of recommendations to strengthen submarine cable infrastructure, which "carries more than 99 per cent of data traffic worldwide". The report names the key challenges as "high exposure to physical risks", "increased time needed for repair", "geographical concentration of infrastructure" and "high dependence of many countries on a small number of cable systems", with the greatest impact on "small island developing states (SIDS), Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and other underserved regions".

ITU's Porto Submarine Cable Resilience Summit release (Porto, 3 February 2026) states: "About 500 of the cables extending more than 1.7 million kilometres serve as the backbone of global connectivity", that "More than 99 per cent of international data traffic is carried by subsea cables", and that "Over 200 faults are reported globally each year" - a slightly higher annual fault figure than the 150-200 range given in the advisory body's July 2026 final report.

published.description: Submarine telecommunications cables carry over 99 per cent of intercontinental data traffic, and 150-200 faults are reported on them every year. Individual faults are routine and usually invisible, because traffic reroutes; the risk is structural. More than 80 per cent of incidents come from commercial fishing gear and dragged ship anchors, repair capacity is thin — about 70 vessels worldwide can repair a cable but only 20-25 are dedicated to it, and Africa has one permanently dedicated repair ship, at Cape Town — and the average repair response time more than doubled between 2012 and 2024, from under 20 days to more than 50. Routes funnel through a few narrow chokepoints: at least 17 cables carrying an estimated 17-20 per cent of global internet traffic pass through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in waters under 14 miles wide. Countries served by a single cable system lose connectivity outright when it breaks, and the ITU-ICPC advisory body on cable resilience closed in July 2026 with recommendations rather than binding obligations.
published.name: Submarine Communications Cable Disruption

assessment.summary: The mechanism here is unusually well understood, which is why the probability is rated high rather than speculative: measles needs about 95 percent two-dose coverage to stop circulating, the world is at 77 percent, and the gap translates into outbreaks with an arithmetic reliability that few other threats on this list offer. What makes it a standing threat rather than a solved problem is that the deficit is not primarily technical — the vaccine is cheap, effective and decades old — but a compound of conflict, disrupted health systems and vaccine hesitancy, each of which erodes coverage faster than campaigns rebuild it. The Americas are the clearest warning, having lost and then regained elimination once already before losing it again in November 2025. Severity is continental: measles and its peers kill tens of thousands a year and can paralyse health systems regionally, but they do not threaten civilizational continuity, and the damage is reversible by the same tool that caused the decline when it went unused.
assessment.timeframe: Under way now: coverage has hovered in the same narrow range since 2009, and elimination status has been withdrawn from four countries in the Americas within twelve months.

claims.text: WHO's measles fact sheet (last updated 15 July 2026) states that "An estimated 95 000 people died from measles in 2024" and that "Measles vaccination averted nearly 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024."

The WHO/UNICEF immunization coverage estimates released 15 July 2026 report 2025 measles coverage "with 84% of children receiving the first measles dose (MCV1) and 77% receiving the second dose (MCV2)", adding that "Both figures fall far short of the 95% threshold required to prevent outbreaks of this highly contagious virus" and that "57 countries reported large or disruptive measles outbreaks in 2025."

The same WHO/UNICEF release states that "an estimated 13.5 million 'zero-dose' children did not receive a single vaccine in their first year during 2025", and that global coverage has been "hovering within the same narrow range since 2009".

PAHO announced on 10 November 2025 that "the Region of the Americas has lost its verification as free from endemic measles transmission" after endemic transmission was re-established in Canada, where the virus had circulated for at least 12 months. As of 7 November 2025 the region had recorded 12 596 confirmed cases across ten countries - about 30 times the 2024 count - and 28 deaths, with second-dose MMR coverage averaging 79 percent in 2024, well below the 95 percent needed to prevent outbreaks.

PAHO's technical reference of 17 November 2026 states that following the sixth annual meeting of the Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission (10-13 November 2026), the United States, Mexico and Bolivia were also found to have lost national measles elimination status, the virus having "circulated continuously in each country for at least 12 months". As of epidemiological week 44 (6 November 2026) "58,213 measles cases have been reported by member countries and territories", with 114 deaths, and regional routine coverage in 2025 "reached only 88% for the first dose of measles vaccine and 85% for the second dose".

PAHO, reporting WHO estimates on 28 November 2025, states that measles caused "an estimated 11 million infections in 2024" and that "an estimated 95 000 people, mostly children younger than 5 years of age, died due to measles in 2024", a fall of 88 percent in deaths between 2000 and 2024, with 59 countries reporting large or disruptive measles outbreaks in 2024.

published.description: Diseases that vaccination had pushed to the margins are returning, because immunisation coverage has stalled well below the level needed to stop them spreading. Measles is the indicator, since it is the most contagious of them and the first to come back when coverage slips: WHO estimates 95 000 deaths and around 11 million infections in 2024, and global coverage in 2025 stood at 84 percent for the first measles dose and 77 percent for the second, far short of the 95 percent needed to prevent outbreaks. An estimated 13.5 million children received no vaccine at all in their first year of life in 2025, and 57 countries reported large or disruptive measles outbreaks. The loss of hard-won ground is already formal: the Americas lost their region-wide measles elimination verification in November 2025, and in November 2026 the regional commission found endemic transmission re-established in the United States, Mexico and Bolivia as well. Vaccination still averted nearly 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024, which is what is being eroded.
published.name: Resurgence of Vaccine-Preventable Disease

assessment.summary: A continent-scale disaster with extremely low annual probability, continuously monitored, and with no current signs of unrest beyond background levels.
assessment.timeframe: No reliable short-term forecast. The three largest past eruptions occurred ~2.1M, ~1.3M, and ~0.64M years ago.

claims.text: The USGS estimates the yearly probability of another Yellowstone caldera-forming eruption at roughly 1 in 730,000 (0.00014%), based on averaging the intervals between the three past major eruptions.

USGS states Yellowstone's three caldera-forming eruptions were the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff (~2.1 million years ago), the Mesa Falls Tuff (~1.3 million years ago), and the Lava Creek Tuff (~640,000 years ago).
The USGS states there is no evidence that a catastrophic eruption at Yellowstone is imminent, and that such events are unlikely to occur in the next few centuries.

The Yellowstone Volcano Observatory's 1 September 2026 monthly update gives the current Volcano Alert Level as NORMAL and the current Aviation Color Code as GREEN, and reports 61 earthquakes located in the Yellowstone National Park region during August 2026, the largest a magnitude 2.0 micro earthquake.

published.description: A large caldera system beneath Yellowstone National Park capable of a 'supereruption' that would blanket much of North America in ash and inject climate-altering aerosols into the stratosphere. Eruptions on that scale are extraordinarily rare: the USGS puts the yearly probability of another caldera-forming eruption at roughly 1 in 730,000 and states there is no evidence one is imminent, or likely within the next few centuries. The Yellowstone Volcano Observatory holds the volcano at its lowest status — Volcano Alert Level NORMAL, Aviation Color Code GREEN — with seismicity at background levels and caldera uplift of about a centimetre or less over recent months.
